headline: County commissioner calls for Flock pause, incoming chief defends cameras — school pilot vote faces uncertain path to Aug. 25
paragraphs: Toledo City Council held a public hearing on June 22 on Ordinance O-286-26, which would authorize spending approximately $14,000 to extend the city's existing agreement with Flock Group Inc. for portable automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) used by the Toledo Police Department's Real Time Crime Center — the same public-safety infrastructure that was operational during the June 6 Old West End Festival mass shooting. Residents voiced concerns at the hearing about privacy and about which communities bear the disproportionate burden of surveillance under the ALPR program. Toledo police and the Lucas County Prosecutor's Office have argued the cameras are a key investigative tool that help track vehicles linked to serious crimes, identify suspects, and build criminal cases. The Blade covered the debate on June 22; 13abc and WTOL reported the hearing and upcoming vote. The council vote is scheduled for the regular June 23 session.

The Toledo vote comes as Flock ALPR contracts face growing national scrutiny: more than 30 cities have canceled Flock contracts in 2026, and Cleveland's Flock camera network is set to go dark on June 29 after the Cleveland City Council rejected an extension. Toledo's existing ALPR program was authorized in November 2025, when council voted to expand use of portable cameras; the June 23 vote is a one-year renewal at minimal cost. The substantive debate — who controls the data, how long records are retained, how enforcement use is audited, and whether the technology produces racially disproportionate outcomes — mirrors what Cleveland and other Ohio cities have confronted. Separately, a broader Ohio privacy debate has accompanied the national Flock backlash, with several state lawmakers examining whether statewide standards for ALPR use are needed.

Toledo City Council voted 8-4 at its June 23 regular session to approve Ordinance O-286-26, extending the portable Flock ALPR contract for one year at $14,000. The Blade reported that council members voting yes said they would not take investigative tools away from Toledo Police, while simultaneously issuing warnings that the technology must not be abused. Four council members voted no. The 8-4 split is the sharpest surveillance governance divide Toledo City Council has produced in recent years, and it arrives as Cleveland's Flock network goes dark June 29 — making Toledo's renewal a regional outlier. The vote keeps the Real Time Crime Center's portable ALPR capability intact through mid-2027; the next renewal cycle will carry the full weight of the post-OWE oversight debate the four dissenting votes signaled.

On August 7, 13abc reported that a Flock ALPR camera near Dorr Street and Joyce Lane in Toledo was cut down and vandalized — a police report documents the pole was severed and the camera unit retrieved by officers and taken to the Criminal Intelligence Section. Police Chief Mike Troendle condemned the act: 'These cameras are an important tool that help solve crimes and provide valuable leads. Damaging these cameras only impacts our ability to investigate crimes and serve our community.' The Toledo incident is part of a documented national pattern: MPR News and CNN both reported in early August that Flock cameras are being vandalized and taken down in protest across multiple jurisdictions; law enforcement agencies nationwide — including Lorain County, Ohio and communities in Franklin County, Ohio — reported widespread ALPR camera vandalism in the same window. Toledo's June 23 contract renewal remains intact; the vandalized unit has been retrieved for assessment.

Toledo police and Oregon police each reported additional Flock ALPR vandalism over the August 15–16 weekend, escalating the local pattern. In Toledo, three cameras were damaged: one near I-280 and Starr Avenue on August 15, and two more on August 16 — one at Burger and Seaman Street and one in the 100 block of Burger Street. In Oregon, two cameras were vandalized along Starr Avenue — poles cut down, camera lenses spray-painted black, and wiring severed. 13abc and WTOL both reported the incidents on August 17. Toledo and Oregon leaders condemned the vandalism. Separately, Toledo City Council is scheduled to vote on August 25 on a proposal by District 2 Council Member Adam Martinez to link exterior cameras at 14 Toledo-area public, private, and Catholic schools — including locations near the CYO athletic complex and Rogers High School Stadium — to the existing Flock ALPR network. Flock Safety has announced new data-governance safeguards that Martinez's office said could influence the council vote outcome. An August 25 approval would allow implementation to begin before year end.

Lucas County Commissioner Pete Gerken called publicly on August 17 for the Sheriff's Office to pause use of Flock ALPR cameras on county property amid the escalating vandalism pattern; Sheriff Mike Navarre responded that suspending the cameras would jeopardize public safety. On August 18, incoming Toledo Police Chief Kevin Braun gave his first public statement on the vandalism, defending Flock technology in notably strong terms: 'probably the most valuable tool that we've ever had in my time here.' Braun's position closely aligns with Chief Troendle's public stance and signals continuity in the department's support for the program through the November 1 leadership transition. Repair and replacement costs for the seven cameras downed across Toledo and Oregon since August 7 are borne by taxpayers; the cumulative damage represents a growing fiscal and operational drain on the Real Time Crime Center's ALPR capability.

Toledo City Council's committee review of the school camera pilot continued August 18–19, ahead of the scheduled August 25 full-council vote. Council member Nick Komives stated the council will take 'a serious look at policy around technology and AI usage' — language suggesting a framework governance discussion rather than a simple yes/no on the pilot. Council member Dr. Brittany Jones characterized the community's concerns as being 'with the company' rather than with the technology itself — a framing that could shape whether the council conditions approval on governance changes rather than rejecting the proposal outright. The school pilot, as currently structured, would cover 16 sites (expanded from the originally reported 14), at approximately $85,000 in year-one costs. The August 25 vote remains on the council calendar; the outcome is uncertain, and any amendment, deferral, or committee referral would push implementation past year end.

Commissioner Gerken held a formal news conference around August 18–19 at which he disclosed a concrete data point underpinning his audit request: Lucas County Flock camera data was searched 904,642 times by 3,241 organizations — including the FBI and out-of-state law enforcement agencies — over a single 30-day period from June 20 to July 20. 'You are being surveilled,' Gerken said, arguing the volume of external access crosses into mass surveillance without sufficient regulatory oversight. WTOL reported Gerken is calling for an independent audit of the program, not merely a temporary pause; Sheriff Navarre explicitly refused the request, saying he has no intention of pausing the cameras or canceling the contract. Council members Komives and Kramer joined Gerken at the news conference in support of the oversight call. The 904K figure gives the four-member dissenting bloc from the June 8-4 vote a concrete data anchor heading into the August 25 school pilot vote.

Despite refusing a pause or audit, Sheriff Navarre approved a formal written use policy governing Lucas County's 33 Flock ALPR cameras on August 19, 2026, and jointly launched a public Transparency Portal with the Toledo Police Department displaying camera locations and search volumes — an institutional response to the governance pressure that stopped short of the oversight Gerken demanded. The Blade reported the policy on August 19. 13abc reported August 20 that the new framework requires deputies to tie every Flock database search to a specific active case, flags unusual or high-volume search patterns for supervisory review, and cuts maximum data retention from 30 days to 7 days. Flock Safety announced these as company-level improvements applicable system-wide; council member Martinez's office acknowledged the governance changes as potentially shaping votes on the August 25 school camera pilot. The four-dissenting-vote bloc has not publicly indicated the new policies satisfy their concerns.
why_it_matters: The August 25 school camera pilot vote — 16 sites, approximately $85,000 in year-one costs — is the proximate governance decision, now four days out. Sheriff Navarre's August 19 transparency portal and formal use policy represent the first concrete institutional concession in the governance debate, but fall short of Commissioner Gerken's call for an independent audit and pause. The vandalism pattern — seven cameras downed across Toledo and Oregon since August 7 — has given the four dissenting council votes from June a sharper platform, while the new data-governance commitments (case-tied searches, 7-day retention) give yes-vote members a new rationale. For economic development, Toledo's ability to market its Real Time Crime Center infrastructure to event organizers, site selectors, and insurance underwriters rests partly on whether the ALPR program is seen as politically stable and durable through the Braun transition. The August 25 vote outcome will set the baseline for how far the next police leadership team can extend the program after November 1.
